1. Approach and rationale

1.1 Central idea

The program is built around a constrained epigraph nonlinear programming strategy. Instead of treating the max overlap by only adding scalar gradient-like steps toward one active lag, the program directly solves a sequence of epigraph subproblems:

- introduce an auxiliary scalar variable \(z\) intended to be a provisional cap on all overlap values;
- impose all, or a selected subset, exact overlap constraints as \(O_\ell(h)-z \le 0\);
- impose the exact equality constraint \(\sum_i h_i=n/2\) and the box constraints \(0\le h_i\le 1\);
- use an analytic Jacobian for the overlap constraints;
- call SciPy's SLSQP method as a warm-start local nonlinear-program solver;
- accept proposals only when repaired points have a strictly better exact objective under the original evaluator.

A secondary engine supplies deterministic descent probes: active-constraint least-squares directions, exact one-dimensional line searches along sum-zero directions, and explicit array transformations such as reversal and complement. These engines are not final proof mechanisms; they are candidate generators. Every returned candidate is certified by the original exact correlation objective.

1.2 Why this can improve the supplied parent

The supplied parent optimizer is essentially a single-point local method: it proposes random, pair, and active-lag directions and performs exact line searches. It can stagnate when several overlap constraints are tied near the current maximum and a useful step must reduce several such constraints simultaneously. The epigraph representation addresses this directly.

The overlap cap \(z\) is not a smooth surrogate. A subproblem can attempt to lower many active rows at once, subject to the same global mass constraint and box constraints that the final evaluator enforces. An epigraph model supplies a multi-constraint local model instead of one scalar active-lag direction. Starting from the supplied parent or its transformations, this structure can make local moves that are more coherent near tied controller minima.

1.3 Important limitations and assumptions

- The problem is nonconvex. SLSQP, active least-squares directions, and the fallback line searches are local or semi-global heuristics. No claim of global optimality is made.
- A successful local numerical solution guarantees only its returned local optimality conditions under tolerance, not a global bound.
- A subset epigraph solve may omit constraints and cannot alone certify validity; only exact evaluation can validate a proposal.
- Floating-point projection can change constraints slightly. Every candidate is repaired and re-exactly evaluated before being stored as best.
- The method may reduce \(\psi(h)\) by only one part in thousands; tight tolerance around tolerance is essential. The plan therefore runs many diversified local solvers and retains only validated improvements.
- If time, memory, or solver behavior threatens the time limit, the scheduler returns the best feasible array already saved and never relies on an unrealized numerical result.

2. Mathematical specification

2.1 Fixed representation and exact objective

For a candidate vector \(h\), define:

\[
n = \operatorname{len}(h),\qquad dx = 2.0/n,
\]
\[
a_r = \operatorname{np.correlate}(h,1.0-h,\textarg="full"),
\]
and the metric vector
\[
s_r = dx\,a_r.
\]
There are \(2n-1\) rows. Define lag
\[
\ell = r-(n-1),\quad \ell\in\{-n+1,\ldots,n-1\}.
\]
For lag \(\ell\), set
\[
A(\ell)=\max(0,\ell),\qquad B(\ell)=\min(n,n+\ell).
\]
Then the exact underlying row formula is
\[
s_\ell(h)=dx\sum_{i=A(\ell)}^{B(\ell)-1} h_i\left(1-h_{i-\ell}\right).
\]
For \(\ell\ge0\), valid terms are equivalently
\[
s_\ell(h)=dx\sum_{j=0}^{n-\ell-1}h_{j+\ell}(1-h_j),
\]
with the full support boundary limiting the sum. For \(\ell=-q\) with \(q>0\),
\[
s_{-q}(h)=dx\sum_{j=0}^{n-q-1}h_j(1-h_{j+q}).
\]
The objective is
\[
\psi(h)=\max_\ell s_\ell(h).
\]
The implementation must also be linear with fanded discrete values that approximate the finite-support correlation and keep all positive and zero negative lags unless evaluating the full evaluator; if replacing in linearization, equations must criticize their restriction and exact acceptance validate the relational necessary dead behavior.

A vector is feasible when:

- \(h_i\) is finite for all \(i\);
- \(0\le h_i\le1\);
- \(\sum_i h_i=n/2\) within tolerance.

2.3 Analytic gradients for the epigraph formulation

The full epigraph constraints use rows:
\[
s_\ell(h)-z\le0,\qquad \ell=-n+1,\ldots,n-1.
\]
At \(x=(h,z)\), derivative of \(s_\ell\) with respect to \(z\) is \(-1\). To compute the derivatives with respect to \(h\), define arrays:
\[
a = np.arange(A(\ell),B(\ell)),
\]
\[
b = a-\ell.
\]
A gradient row \(g^{(\ell)}\) is:
- initialize \(g\) length \(n\) to zero;
- for all valid terms with indices \((a_k,b_k)\):
  \[
  g[a_k] \leftarrow g[a_k] + dx(1-h_{b_k}),
  \]
  \[
  g[b_k] \leftarrow g[b_k] - dx\,h_{a_k}.
  \]
The constrain Jacobian row is therefore the concatenation of this \(g^{(\ell)}\) with the final derivative \(-1\).
